acceptance_criteria.statement: Submitting a long URL returns a short code for that URL.
Requesting a short code that was previously issued redirects the caller to the original long URL that was submitted.
Submitting a long URL together with a custom alias returns a link whose short code is that alias, and requesting that alias redirects to the original long URL.
Requesting a custom alias that is already in use does not overwrite or redirect to the existing link, and the caller is told the alias is unavailable.
Submitting a long URL together with an expiry produces a link that redirects before the expiry and no longer redirects after the expiry has passed.
Requesting a short code that has never been issued returns 404.
Looking up statistics for an existing short code returns basic statistics for that link.
Looking up statistics for a short code that does not exist returns 404.
Deleting an existing short code succeeds, and subsequently requesting that short code no longer redirects.
Deleting a short code that does not exist returns 404.
A submitted value that is not a usable URL is rejected with a client error rather than producing a short code.
Links created by the service survive a restart of the application (state is held in PostgreSQL, not in memory).

constraints: The service runs behind the company's edge proxy and must not implement authentication itself
Scope is the 'core APIs' — the deliverable is an HTTP API, not a UI
The repository currently contains no application source or build files beyond the requirement input; this is a greenfield implementation of the stated stack
No deadline is stated in the requirement
output.goal: Users can shorten a long URL into a short code that redirects to the original URL, optionally with a custom alias and an expiry, and can look up basic statistics for a link they created or delete it.
in_scope: Submitting a long URL and receiving a short code in return
Visiting a short code and being redirected to the original long URL
Optionally supplying a custom alias when creating a link
Optionally supplying an expiry when creating a link
Looking up basic statistics for a link the caller created
Behaviour when a short code is unknown, expired, or a requested custom alias is already taken
non_functional: Redirect requests are on the end-user hot path and are expected to be low latency
Short codes must be unique across all live links
Redirect behaviour must be safe against concurrent creation of the same custom alias
Redirect targets are attacker-supplied URLs, so stored and returned values must be handled without introducing injection or open-redirect-abuse beyond the intended redirect
The service is expected to be operable behind the edge proxy: it should start against a configured PostgreSQL instance and expose enough logging/observability to diagnose failed redirects
Redirect availability matters more than creation availability, since broken redirects break already-published links
No explicit throughput, latency, or uptime targets were stated in the requirement
out_of_scope: Authentication and authorisation — the requirement states the edge proxy handles authentication, and the service does not
Identifying or establishing who 'created' a link (the requirement references links 'they created' but specifies no caller identity mechanism)
A user interface, web console, or admin UI
Editing or updating an existing link (only create, redirect, stats, delete are asked for)
Listing or searching a caller's links
Rate limiting, abuse prevention, spam or malicious-URL filtering
Analytics beyond the unspecified 'basic statistics' (e.g. referrer, geo, per-device breakdowns)
Bulk creation or import/export of links
QR code generation, link previews, or vanity domains
Deployment, infrastructure, edge proxy configuration, and CI/CD setup
API versioning and public API documentation deliverables

As written, any caller who knows or guesses a short code can read its statistics and permanently delete it, including links published by someone else. Should the service enforce ownership on stats and delete, and if so, from what identity source (e.g. a trusted header injected by the edge proxy)? (escalated to human, not failed)

answers.Q1: Yes, enforce ownership. The edge proxy authenticates and injects X-User-Id. The service trusts that header, records it as the link owner on creation, and requires it on stats and delete: absent or blank header on those routes is 401, and a code owned by someone else is 404 rather than 403, so the stats endpoint cannot be used to probe for codes the caller does not own. GET /{code} redirects stay public and unauthenticated. Version the management API under /api/v1; the redirect stays at the root, unversioned, because a short link is pasted into the world and can never be migrated.

payload.note: Behind the edge proxy, as stated. Trust the injected identity header; do not invent auth in the service. Same decision as greenfield-1.

output.blast_radius: This is genuinely greenfield on this branch: `git ls-files service` returns six scaffold files, there are no controllers, entities, repositories, or migrations, and no caller anywhere — in this repository or outside it — currently depends on a short code resolving. Nothing can regress in the usual sense because nothing yet runs. The real risk is therefore not to existing consumers but to the scaffold's already-made decisions, and it concentrates in two places. First, the redirect cache: `@EnableCaching` is already on and `CacheConfig` declares a five-minute in-process Caffeine cache that its own javadoc says also caches negative lookups. If the implementation caches the wrong thing, deleted and expired links keep redirecting — the worst plausible failure here is a link that was deliberately taken down still sending traffic to an attacker-supplied URL for minutes after the delete returned 204, on every instance except the one that handled the delete. A single-instance test suite will not see it, and the only way anyone finds out is a user report or someone noticing redirect metrics for a code that no longer exists. Second, config and schema: `ddl-auto: validate` over an empty migration directory means the first entity/migration disagreement takes down context load for the entire test suite at once, and A12's required `app.base-url` is absent from application.yml, docker-compose.yml, and ci.yml, so introducing it as mandatory breaks CI and local boot simultaneously and presents as a code defect. Both of those are loud and immediate, which makes them far cheaper than the cache problem. Weighting for review: the cache-versus-delete interaction and the migration deserve careful human attention; the rest of the surface is new code with no incumbent behaviour behind it and can be reviewed on its merits. One process note worth surfacing rather than burying — the change necessarily touches three protected paths (`application.yml`, `db/migration/**`, and potentially `pom.xml`), each of which forces PENDING_APPROVAL, so the approval should be planned into `design` rather than tripped over during `implement`. And Q1 (ownership of stats and delete) is still marked blocking: as written, any caller who guesses a code can permanently delete someone else's live link, and A5's no-reissue rule makes that irreversible. Branch `sdlc/greenfield-1` answered it with an `X-User-Id` header and a 401, but that is a prior run's choice, not a decision recorded for this one.

breaking_changes.detail: A12 specifies the short URL is built from a configured app.base-url that 'fails loudly at startup' if absent. Neither service/src/main/resources/application.yml, nor docker-compose.yml, nor .github/workflows/ci.yml supplies it. Adding it as required breaks three things that work today: the CI 'service' job (./mvnw -B verify at context load), the documented 'docker compose up' walkthrough in IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md §11, and every subclass of AbstractIntegrationTest — which is the whole test suite, since @SpringBootTest loads the full context. It would surface as a mass ApplicationContextException, i.e. as a code defect rather than a config gap.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Add app.base-url to application.yml in the same commit as the code that reads it, defaulting to ${APP_BASE_URL:http://localhost:8080} so the compose and CI paths keep working, and let the deployed environment override via APP_BASE_URL. If it must be genuinely required in production, keep the placeholder but add a @Validated @NotBlank on the properties bean and set an explicit test value in the test context. Note that touching application.yml is a protected-path write and will force PENDING_APPROVAL — that approval should be requested deliberately at design rather than discovered at implement.
breaking_changes.surface: Application startup — app.base-url as a required property with no default (A12)

breaking_changes.detail: This is the answer to 'can old and new run at the same time': no, not safely, for delete and expiry. CacheConfig's 'links' cache is in-process Caffeine with expireAfterWrite=5m. During any rolling deploy, or on any multi-instance deployment, instance A processing DELETE /api/links/{code} can only evict its own local cache. Instance B continues serving 302s to the deleted target for up to five minutes, and AC9 says the code must not redirect subsequently. Expiry has a milder version of the same problem if the expiry check is baked into the cached value rather than evaluated per request. A single-instance acceptance test will pass while the production behaviour is wrong, which is the worst combination.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Cache only the immutable part of the row (short code -> target URL plus the expires_at instant) and evaluate expires_at <= now() per request outside the cache, so expiry needs no invalidation at all. For delete, either (a) accept and document a bounded staleness window and cut app.cache.spec expireAfterWrite to a value the requester agrees to, or (b) do not cache at all until a shared invalidation channel exists — Redis pub/sub is already named in CacheConfig's javadoc and IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md §7 as the documented scale path, not a current dependency. Whichever is chosen, state it in the delete endpoint's contract; 'the link stops redirecting immediately' is not currently deliverable on more than one instance. Do not silently rely on a local LinkCacheInvalidator and call AC9 satisfied.
breaking_changes.surface: Redirect correctness under the existing Caffeine cache — AC5 and AC9 across instances

breaking_changes.detail: Adding a root-level @GetMapping("/{code}") introduces a handler for the whole single-segment path space of a context that already serves /error (Spring's BasicErrorController, reachable because server.error is configured in application.yml) and /actuator. Spring's more-specific-mapping precedence means the framework paths generally win, so the real breakage runs the other way: an alias of 'error' or 'actuator' is well-formed under A7's ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$, is accepted with 201, is persisted, permanently consumes that code under A5's no-reissue rule, and then never redirects. The caller is told the link was created and it silently does not work.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Extend the reserved set beyond A1's '/api/ prefix and actuator paths' to explicitly include 'error', 'actuator', and 'favicon.ico', reject a reserved alias at create time with the same 400 A7 uses for a malformed alias, and exclude reserved words from the generated-code path too. Make the reserved list a configuration property so it can be extended without a code change, and add an integration test that POSTs alias 'error' and asserts 400 — otherwise this regresses invisibly.
breaking_changes.surface: Root path routing — /error and /actuator shadowed by GET /{code}

breaking_changes.detail: application.yml sets spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate and db/migration currently holds only .gitkeep. Once an @Entity exists, any mismatch between it and V1 (column name, nullability, type — notably timestamptz vs timestamp for A9's UTC instants, and Postgres lower-casing unquoted identifiers) fails context load for every test class, not just the one under test. Branch sdlc/greenfield-1 is the precedent: it produced 20+ implementation classes including a Link entity and never wrote a migration at all, so its db/migration still contains only .gitkeep.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Treat the migration as part of the same unit of work as the entity and write it first, not last. Have the design node fix column names, types, and nullability in the frozen contract so implement cannot drift from them. Because implement and author-tests run in separate worktrees and only the former can write src/main/resources, the migration must not be deferred to a follow-up node. The existing theApplicationContextLoads test is the cheapest early detector — if it fails, nothing else in the suite means anything.
breaking_changes.surface: Test-suite schema validation — ddl-auto: validate against the first Flyway migration

impacted.notes: The single most load-bearing pre-existing decision. Declares a Caffeine cache named 'links' with spec 'maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=5m', and its javadoc states it 'Caches negative lookups too'. UrlShortenerApplication already carries @EnableCaching, so the cache is live the moment a @Cacheable resolver is added. The file itself need not change, but AC5 (stops redirecting after expiry) and AC9 (subsequently no longer redirects) are both directly falsifiable by a 5-minute write-expiry cache: a deleted or expired link keeps redirecting from cache. Caffeine is in-process, so eviction is per-instance only. Prior run branch sdlc/greenfield-1 needed CachedLinkResolver + LinkCacheInvalidator to cope; that pairing is the integration point, not an optional optimisation.

Protected path (orchestrator/pipelines/sdlc.yaml policy.protected_paths lists 'service/src/main/resources/application*.yml') so any write forces PENDING_APPROVAL regardless of node autonomy. A12 requires an app.base-url property that does not exist here today; the file currently defines only app.cache.spec under the 'app' namespace. Also sets spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate, which turns any entity/migration mismatch into a context-load failure rather than a silent schema drift, and server.error.include-message: never, which suppresses messages on the default error path and interacts with A14's RFC 7807 bodies (ProblemDetail from an @ExceptionHandler is unaffected; framework-generated 400s are).

Directory contains only .gitkeep — there is no V1 migration and Flyway has never run against this schema. This is the first migration the repository has ever had, and with ddl-auto: validate it is the gating artifact for context startup in every integration test. Protected path (db/migration/**) so writing it forces PENDING_APPROVAL. The unique index on the short-code column is the mechanism A8 relies on to resolve alias contention (insert-then-translate-23505, not read-then-write), and A5's soft delete means deleted_at must be nullable and must NOT be part of the unique key, or a retired code becomes reissuable and contradicts A5/Q6.

Unchanged, but its @SpringBootApplication component scan roots at com.example.urlshortener, so every new package (create, redirect, stats, delete, domain, web) is auto-registered with no wiring edit. Its @EnableCaching is what makes CacheConfig active. Javadoc explicitly records that everything below it in the package tree is orchestrator output — i.e. the greenfield boundary is documented in-tree.

The only existing test, and the only hand-written file under src/test. Its POSTGRES container is static, so one PostgreSQL is shared by every test class in the run with no truncation between them — hit counts, alias uniqueness, and soft-deleted rows leak across classes unless tests randomise codes. Its theApplicationContextLoads test currently passes trivially and will start exercising Flyway the moment a migration lands. Note a conflict with Q7's proposed answer: @ServiceConnection hard-binds the container, so an 'external datasource URL' escape hatch requires editing this file, which implement's deny_paths forbid (service/src/test/**) and only author-tests may write.

A1 puts the redirect at the root, which makes it a catch-all over the entire single-segment path space of an already-running Spring context. It collides with Spring's BasicErrorController at /error and with the actuator base path /actuator, both single-segment and both live today per application.yml management.endpoints.web.exposure. A7's alias grammar ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$ admits 'error' and 'actuator', so those aliases can be created (201) yet never redirect — a silent AC3 failure. A1 reserves only the /api/ prefix and 'actuator paths'; /error is not covered by either and needs adding to the reserved set.

Should not need to change: the dependency set already covers everything the assumptions require — web, data-jpa, validation, actuator, cache, caffeine, flyway-core + flyway-database-postgresql, postgresql, micrometer-registry-prometheus, spring-boot-testcontainers, testcontainers/postgresql + junit-jupiter. Flagged because it is both a protected path and in implement's deny_paths, and it is frozen by design; a node discovering a missing dependency mid-branch cannot add it without escalating. Notably absent: spring-boot-starter-security, consistent with auth being out of scope, which means Q1's ownership option has no framework support to lean on.

The committed plan of record (§7) specifies a contract that the frozen assumptions contradict on five points: POST /api/v1/links (versioned) vs A1's /api/links; '410 expired vs 404 unknown' vs A4's uniform 404; an Idempotency-Key header vs A13's no-dedupe; SSRF rejection of private/loopback/link-local ranges and self-referential hosts vs A6's scheme allowlist only; transactional outbox analytics vs A11's fire-and-forget UPDATE. §5 does list 'idempotency key, negative caching' as cuttable, but the versioning and 410 divergences are not covered by that. Whichever way it is resolved, this document and the code will disagree unless the docs node reconciles them. OPERATIONS.md also records that greenfield-1's contract was rejected by a human specifically over API versioning.

Unchanged, but goes from near-vacuous to load-bearing. Its 'service' job runs ./mvnw -B verify, which today starts a Postgres container and asserts only that the context loads; once a migration and real tests exist it exercises Flyway, the unique index, and the redirect path on every push and PR. It sets no DB_URL or app.base-url env, so a config property that is required-with-no-default (A12) fails this job at context load.

Protected path. Provides postgres:17-alpine with db/user/password 'shortener', matching application.yml's DB_URL default, so local boot works unchanged. It injects no app.base-url, so the same startup-failure exposure as CI applies to the documented 'docker compose up' walkthrough in IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md §11.

Prometheus scrape surface already exposed and micrometer-registry-prometheus is already a runtime dependency, so any new counters/timers on the redirect path appear in /actuator/prometheus automatically and become a surface someone can alert on from first deploy. Health probes are enabled (management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true); adding Flyway plus a datasource-backed repository puts DB reachability into the readiness signal. No alert rules exist in this repository, so nothing is being renamed out from under an existing alert — this is new operational surface, not changed surface.

New end-to-end flow with no existing readers: POST /api/links writes a link row; GET /{code} reads it through the Caffeine cache; the redirect then issues A11's fire-and-forget hit-count UPDATE against the same row; GET /api/links/{code}/stats reads hit_count and last_accessed_at back. Two things to hold onto: the stats read and the async counter write race, so stats are eventually-consistent by construction (A11 accepts this); and the counter UPDATE touches the same row the redirect just read, so a naive @Transactional wrapper would put a write on the hot path and invert the stated latency/availability priority. Nothing else in the repository reads this table — no reports, exports, or other services exist.

Read-only for this node (orchestrator/** is a forbidden path) but its gates change meaning. coverage_floor min_line_coverage 0.70 is currently measured against two scaffold classes and becomes a real constraint. routes_match_openapi is documented in OPERATIONS.md as a regex scan of Spring annotations, not an AST walk: it handles literal-string mappings, so @GetMapping("/{code}") is fine, but it will not catch a route composed dynamically or one declared via a base-path property.

regression_surface: AbstractIntegrationTest.theApplicationContextLoads — the only test that exists today. It must still pass once the first Flyway migration and the first @Entity land, since ddl-auto: validate turns any column name/type/nullability mismatch into a context-load failure for every test class at once.

Redirect after DELETE: create a link, GET /{code} once to populate the Caffeine 'links' cache, DELETE /api/links/{code}, then immediately GET /{code} again — must be 404, not a cached 302. The same sequence with a second application instance is the case a single-instance test cannot cover.

Redirect after expiry: create a link with expires_at a few seconds out, GET /{code} to populate the cache, wait past the expiry, GET again — must be 404 without waiting for the 5-minute expireAfterWrite window.

Negative caching and enumeration: GET /{code} for a never-issued code returns 404, then that same code is later successfully created as a custom alias and must redirect immediately, not serve a cached 404 for up to five minutes.

Reserved-path shadowing: /actuator/health, /actuator/prometheus, and /error must all still respond as they do today after the root-level GET /{code} mapping is added; and POST /api/links with alias 'error' or 'actuator' must be rejected rather than accepted-then-broken.

Application startup with only the defaults present in application.yml and docker-compose.yml — no APP_BASE_URL, no DB_URL override — which is exactly what the CI 'service' job and the documented 'docker compose up' walkthrough do.

CI pipeline end to end: ./mvnw -B verify green, JaCoCo line coverage at or above the 0.70 floor enforced by the coverage_floor gate, and routes_match_openapi agreeing with the frozen OpenAPI — remembering it is a regex scan over literal-string Spring annotations, so a dynamically composed path would pass the gate while being wrong.

Concurrent creation of the same custom alias (A8): two simultaneous POSTs with an identical alias must yield exactly one 201 and one 409 via the unique-constraint violation, with no lost update and no opaque 500. This is the behaviour the unique index in V1 exists to provide.

Soft-delete no-reissue (A5/Q6): after a code is deleted or expires, neither the generator nor a custom-alias create may reclaim it — verify the unique index still covers deleted rows and was not made partial on deleted_at IS NULL.

Hit counting under A11: the counter increments only on requests that actually redirect (not on 404s, expired links, or stats calls), and a failure in the fire-and-forget UPDATE must not turn a successful redirect into a 5xx.

Stats read-back consistency: GET /api/links/{code}/stats returns the six A10 fields, with expires_at and last_accessed_at as UTC instants consistent with hibernate.jdbc.time_zone: UTC and A9's timestamptz storage.
Error body shape: 400/404/409 return RFC 7807 application/problem+json per A14, and are not flattened by server.error.include-message: never on the framework-generated error path.

Approver `neil`, decision `approved`.

A9's timestamptz choice does not need special mapping.

evidence.claim: A8's insert-then-translate strategy works: a second insert of the same code against a plain (non-partial) UNIQUE INDEX raises org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException, rooted in org.postgresql.util.PSQLException 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint "ux_links_code"' with the constraint name recoverable from the server error. So 409 can be distinguished from any other integrity failure by constraint name.

evidence.claim: A root-level @GetMapping("/{code}") does NOT shadow /error or the actuator endpoints. With the controller mapped, GET /error still returns BasicErrorController's response and GET /actuator, GET /actuator/health both return 200 application/vnd.spring-boot.actuator.v3+json. The exposure is the opposite direction: an alias of 'error' or 'actuator' would be accepted at create and could never redirect.

evidence.claim: /favicon.ico DOES reach the root {code} handler (Spring Boot 3.x ships no default favicon handler), returning the controller's 404. Harmless under A7's grammar (a dot is not in ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$) but it means browser traffic pollutes any negative cache.

evidence.claim: A14 ('errors are returned as RFC 7807 application/problem+json') is FALSE by default for framework-generated errors. With server.error.include-message: never, a bean-validation failure, a malformed JSON body and a wrong HTTP method all return application/json DefaultErrorAttributes ({timestamp,status,error,path}), not problem+json. Only errors produced by an @ExceptionHandler returning ProblemDetail come back as application/problem+json.
evidence.source: Live probe, defaults: PROBE|validation-fail|status=400|ctype=application/json|body={"timestamp":...,"status":400,"error":"Bad Request","path":"/api/links"}; PROBE|malformed-json same; PROBE|wrong-method|status=405 same; versus PROBE|redirect-unknown|status=404|ctype=application/problem+json from the @RestControllerAdvice

evidence.claim: Setting spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true does convert framework errors to RFC 7807: 400 'Invalid request content.', 400 'Failed to read request', 405 'Method PUT is not supported.', 404 'No static resource a/b.' all come back as application/problem+json. That property lives in application.yml — a protected path outside design's write_paths — so the code-only alternative is a @RestControllerAdvice extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler.

options.summary: Redirect cache: do not use @Cacheable at all for this deliverable. The redirect is a single indexed lookup on a unique btree against a pooled connection; CacheConfig stays as an unused bean (harmless — @EnableCaching with no cacheable method changes nothing). AC5 and AC9 then hold on any number of instances with no invalidation channel, and the cache can be added later behind a measurement rather than an assumption.

Redirect cache: cache only the immutable pair code -> (target_url, expires_at), evaluate expires_at <= now() per request outside the cache, and evict locally on delete with app.cache.spec's expireAfterWrite cut to a staleness window the requester agrees to. Correct for expiry on any topology; correct for delete only on a single instance, so the delete contract must state the bounded staleness explicitly.

Redirect cache: keep Caffeine and add a shared invalidation channel (Redis pub/sub, named in CacheConfig's javadoc and IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN §7 as the scale path). Rejected as impractical here rather than wrong: it needs a new dependency in pom.xml, which is frozen at design and in implement's deny_paths, plus an operational dependency that is out of scope.

RFC 7807 (A14): implement a @RestControllerAdvice extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler so framework-generated 400/404/405 become problem+json alongside the hand-thrown ones. Pure src/main/java, writable by design, no protected-path approval, and it works regardless of server.error.include-message.

RFC 7807 (A14): set spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true in application.yml. Verified to work, but application.yml is a protected path outside design's write_paths, so it can only be written by implement mid-branch and forces PENDING_APPROVAL there.

payload.detail: all 12 acceptance criterion/a covered by the plan

risks: The human answer recorded for this run (runs/greenfield-2/journal.jsonl seq 13) overrides assumption A1 on two points: management routes sit under /api/v1, and ownership is enforced via a trusted X-User-Id header with 401 when absent and 404 on mismatch. A1's unversioned /api/links shape is exactly what the same approver rejected in greenfield-1. If design emits the A1 shape, routes_match_openapi still passes (it only compares code to contract) and the divergence is not caught until the human design approval, costing a full xhigh re-run and invalidating author-tests' blind URLs.

The pre-existing Caffeine 'links' cache (expireAfterWrite=5m, negative caching per its own javadoc) can falsify AC5 and AC9 while a single-instance test suite stays green: after a DELETE returns 204, another instance keeps serving 302s to an attacker-supplied URL for up to five minutes. U3 (multi-instance? rolling deploy?) is unanswered, so T8 deliberately does not put the cache on the correctness path. If someone reintroduces @Cacheable for latency, AC9 becomes undeliverable without an invalidation channel that pom.xml is frozen against.

ddl-auto: validate turns any entity/migration mismatch into a context-load failure for every test class at once, not a localised failure. Postgres lower-cases unquoted identifiers and timestamptz vs timestamp is a real mismatch source. This is why T2 ships the migration and entity together rather than deferring the migration; greenfield-1 produced 20+ classes and never wrote V1 at all.

app.base-url does not exist anywhere in the repository today. Introducing it as required-with-no-default breaks the CI 'service' job, the documented docker compose walkthrough, and every @SpringBootTest simultaneously, presenting as a mass ApplicationContextException that reads as a code defect. T3 uses ${APP_BASE_URL:http://localhost:8080} with @NotBlank validation instead.

Three protected paths must be written for this change: service/src/main/resources/application.yml, service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_links.sql, and potentially service/pom.xml. Only `implement` may write the resources ones, and design's write_paths exclude them, so the PENDING_APPROVAL lands mid-parallel-branch. Greenfield-1 hit exactly this (paths_confined outcome=escalate). The approval should be anticipated at design rather than tripped over.

A root-level GET /{code} does not shadow /error or /actuator (verified by spike), but the reverse exposure is real: an alias of 'error', 'actuator', or 'api' is well-formed under A7, is accepted with 201, permanently consumes that code under A5's no-reissue rule, and never redirects. T5's reserved-word list plus T13's assertion are the only things preventing a silently broken link.

A14's problem+json claim is false by default for framework-generated errors under the current application.yml (server.error.include-message: never yields DefaultErrorAttributes, not problem+json). Any test asserting problem+json on a bean-validation 400 fails unless T12's advice extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. author-tests writes those assertions blind against the contract, so a contract that promises problem+json without T12 produces a branch mismatch that only surfaces at verify.

postgres:17-alpine is not cached locally and the agent sandbox blocks /var/run/docker.sock, so agent nodes cannot run mvn verify themselves and the first deterministic verify pays a registry pull inside the 1800s timeout. A Docker-group or network gap will present as a whole failing suite rather than an environment problem; Q7's 'external datasource URL' escape hatch does not exist without editing AbstractIntegrationTest, which only author-tests may write.

The Testcontainers PostgreSQL container is static and shared by every test class with no truncation between them, so hit counts, alias uniqueness, and soft-deleted rows leak across classes. Tests that reuse fixed short codes will pass alone and fail in suite order.

The stats read (T10) and the fire-and-forget counter write (T9) race by construction, so stats are eventually consistent. A test that redirects once and immediately asserts hit_count == 1 will be flaky unless it awaits the increment.

U6 is unanswered: docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md §7 is the committed plan of record and contradicts the frozen assumptions on 410-vs-404, idempotency, SSRF filtering, and outbox analytics. Until T16 runs, the repository documents a contract the code does not implement.
